steps.body: On a graph, the **vertical line test** checks the one-output rule visually: if any vertical line crosses the graph more than once, that single x-input has two y-outputs — so it's NOT a function. Cross at most once everywhere means it IS a function.
Sweep a vertical scanner across a continuous relation and record intersection counts.

widget.prompt: Sweep the vertical line across the circle. Record the greatest number of intersections, then decide whether the relation is a function.
widget.successFeedback: Not a function: some vertical lines hit the circle twice, so one input has two outputs.
widget.moreSweepFeedback: Sweep farther. A verdict needs evidence from across the relation, not one convenient x-value.
widget.verdictFeedback: The one-output rule fails wherever the scanner records two intersections.

predict.prompt: A vertical line marks ONE input. If it crosses a graph at two points, that input has how many outputs?
predict.reveal: Both crossings share that x but carry different y's — one input, two answers. The vertical line test just makes the contradiction visible.

cml.actionGoal: Use a continuous scanner to connect intersection count with one-output-per-input.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the relation so every vertical line has at most one hit. What structural change was necessary?

explanation.prompt: What does the scanner count represent?

options.label: How many outputs share the current input.
options.feedback: Exactly — a vertical line fixes one x-value.

options.label: How many inputs share one output.
options.feedback: The scanner fixes x, so it counts outputs for one input.

steps.body: Why does it work? A vertical line is all the points with the same x-value. If the graph meets that line twice, the single x has two y's — exactly the non-function pattern. A straight line (other than a vertical one) always passes the test.

explanationVariants: A slanted straight line is met by any vertical line exactly once, so it passes and IS a function.
Every vertical line crosses a slanted line just once — one output per input.

widget.prompt: Does a slanted straight line (like y = 2x) pass the vertical line test?

options.label: Yes — every vertical line crosses it exactly once
options.feedback: Right — one crossing per vertical line means one output per input.

options.label: No — lines can't be functions
options.feedback: Most lines ARE functions — a slanted line passes the vertical line test easily.

options.label: Only if it goes through the origin
options.feedback: Passing through the origin isn't required — any slanted line passes the test.

options.label: Only if the slope is positive
options.feedback: Slope direction doesn't matter — both uphill and downhill slanted lines pass.

widget.prompt: Does a VERTICAL line (like x = 3) pass the vertical line test?

options.label: No — one x-value has infinitely many y-outputs
options.feedback: Right — a vertical line IS a vertical line, so it overlaps one and gives every y for that x — not a function.

options.label: Yes — it's a straight line
options.feedback: Being straight isn't enough — a vertical line has one x mapping to every y, so it fails.

options.label: Yes — vertical lines are the simplest
options.feedback: Simple or not, a vertical line fails: its single x-value has infinitely many outputs.

options.label: Only if it crosses the x-axis
options.feedback: Crossing the x-axis doesn't change it — a vertical line always fails the test.

explanationVariants: A sideways U (opening right) is crossed twice by many vertical lines, so it FAILS — not a function.
Two crossings on one vertical line means one x maps to two y's.

widget.prompt: A sideways U-shape (opening to the right) — does it pass the vertical line test?

options.label: No — many vertical lines cross it twice
options.feedback: Right — a sideways U gives two y-outputs for many x-values, so it fails.

options.label: Yes — it's a smooth curve
options.feedback: Smoothness isn't the test — the sideways U is crossed twice by vertical lines, so it fails.

options.label: Yes — U-shapes are always functions
options.feedback: An UPRIGHT U (like y=x²) passes, but a SIDEWAYS U fails — direction matters here.

options.label: Only near the tip
options.feedback: Even away from the tip, vertical lines cross a sideways U twice — it fails overall.

explanationVariants: An upright U (like y = x²) is crossed exactly once by every vertical line, so it PASSES and is a function.
Each x-value on an upright parabola has just one y, so it passes the test.

widget.prompt: An upright U-shape (like y = x², opening upward) — does it pass the vertical line test?

options.label: Yes — every vertical line crosses it exactly once
options.feedback: Right — each x gives exactly one y on an upright parabola.

options.label: No — it curves too much
options.feedback: Curving is fine — what matters is that each vertical line crosses only once, which it does.

options.label: No — U-shapes never pass
options.feedback: An upright U passes; only a SIDEWAYS U fails. Direction is the key difference.

options.label: Only at the bottom point
options.feedback: It passes everywhere — every vertical line meets an upright parabola exactly once.

steps.body: Sort graphs by the vertical line test.
explanationVariants: Pass (functions): slanted line, upright U, horizontal line. Fail: vertical line, sideways U — each crossed more than once by some vertical line.
Imagine sweeping a vertical line across each graph: more than one crossing anywhere means it fails.

widget.prompt: Sort each graph: passes the vertical line test or fails?

items.label: a slanted straight line
items.feedback: Crossed once by every vertical line — passes.

items.label: a vertical line
items.feedback: One x-value, infinitely many y's — fails.

items.label: an upright U (y = x²)
items.feedback: Each x gives one y — passes.

items.label: a sideways U (opening right)
items.feedback: Many vertical lines cross it twice — fails.

items.label: a horizontal line
items.feedback: Each x gives exactly one y (always the same) — passes.

widget.missFeedback: Not quite — imagine a vertical line sweeping across each graph. Does it ever cross more than once?
widget.successFeedback: All sorted — passing means every vertical line crosses at most once.

hints: Picture sweeping a vertical line across each graph from left to right.
If the vertical line ever crosses the graph twice at once, that graph fails.
Pass: slanted line, upright U, horizontal line. Fail: vertical line, sideways U.

steps.body: The vertical line test turns the one-output rule into something you can see.
takeaways: Cross more than once → two outputs for one input → NOT a function.
Cross at most once everywhere → IS a function.
Vertical lines and sideways U's fail; slanted lines and upright U's pass.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: rate of change — how fast a function's output climbs.

concept.body: The vertical line test: if any vertical line crosses a graph more than once, that x-value has two outputs, so it's NOT a function. At most one crossing everywhere means it IS a function.

explanationVariants: A horizontal line is crossed exactly once by every vertical line, so it passes — a function.
Each x on a horizontal line has one y (always the same), so it passes the test.

widget.prompt: Does a horizontal line pass the vertical line test?

options.label: Yes — every vertical line crosses it exactly once
options.feedback: Right — one y-output per x, so it's a function.

options.label: No — it's flat
options.feedback: Flatness is fine — a horizontal line gives one output per input, so it passes.

options.label: No — horizontal lines aren't functions
options.feedback: They ARE functions — each x maps to one (constant) y.

options.label: Only if it's above the x-axis
options.feedback: Position doesn't matter — a horizontal line always passes.
